pr_body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
1. Adds `kube-proxy --nodeport-addresses primary`, which tells kube-proxy to only listen for NodePort connections (and HealthCheckNodePort connections) on the node's primary IP(s)
2. Adds a warning at kube-proxy startup if you pass no `--nodeport-addresses`
3. Adds a warning at kube-proxy startup if you pass a single-stack `--nodeport-addresses` but appear to have a dual-stack cluster.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #122899
Fixes #111863
(In both cases, that's "fixes" in the sense of "logs a warning if you are experiencing that bug, which we can't actually fix without potentially breaking other users")

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
This ends up reverting the API-change part of #122724; that PR made `proxyutil.NodePortAddresses` implement this functionality itself, which worked when we always wanted the behavior for nftables and never for the other backends. But if we want it to be _optional_ for the other backends, it turns out to be easier to just implement it by just passing an appropriate `nodePortAddresses []string` to the constructor instead.

The first commit ("Remove an unused type...") was something I noticed while implementing this in a different way that I then changed my mind about, so it ends up being pretty much irrelevant to this PR, but :man_shrugging: 

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
The kube-proxy nodeportAddresses / --nodeport-addresses option now
accepts the value "primary", meaning to only listen for NodePort connections
on the node's primary IPv4 and/or IPv6 address (according to the Node object).
This is strongly recommended, if you were not previously using
--nodeport-addresses, to avoid surprising behavior.

(This behavior is enabled by default with the nftables backend; you would
need to explicitly request `--nodeport-addresses 0.0.0.0/0,::/0` there to get
the traditional "listen on all interfaces" behavior.)
```

/kind bug
/kind cleanup
/sig network
/priority important-longterm
cc @nayihz

# On Node IPs and LoadBalancers

Terminology note for the discussion below:
- primary node IPs: the IP or IPs returned from `utilnode.GetNodeHostIPs()`
- primary node IP: the first/only IP returned from `utilnode.GetNodeHostIPs()`
- secondary node IP: the optional second IP returned from `utilnode.GetNodeHostIPs()`, in a dual-stack cluster

### GCE
[`node.Status.Addresses` is constructed as](https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-gcp/blob/providers/v0.28.2/providers/gce/gce_instances.go#L112-L180):
- for each NIC:
  - append the NIC's private IPv4 IP as an InternalIP
  - if the NIC has IPv6 IPs then append the first IPv6 IP (whether public or private) as an InternalIP
  - if the NIC has external IPs than append the first (IPv4?) external IP as an ExternalIP
- append the hostname as InternalDNS and HostName

So GetNodeHostIPs will return the private IPv4 IP of the first NIC as the primary node IP. In a dual-stack cluster, it will also return the first IPv6 IP of the first NIC that has an IPv6 IP as the secondary node IP. (GCE thus does not currently support single-stack IPv6 or "IPv6-primary" dual-stack.)

LoadBalancers are pointed at VMs. The [GCE docs](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/backend-service#backend_vms_and_external_ip_addresses) say:

> GFEs communicate with backend VMs or endpoints by sending packets to an internal address created by joining an identifier for the backend's VPC network with the internal IPv4 address of the backend.

and

> For instance group backends, the internal IPv4 address is always the primary internal IPv4 address that corresponds to the nic0 interface of the VM.

So on GCE, LBs always send to the IP that we consider to be the primary node IP.

### AWS

[`node.Status.Addresses` is constructed as](https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-aws/blob/v1.30.0-rc.0/pkg/providers/v1/aws.go#L1669-L1688)
- (the order of the IPv4 and IPv6 steps depends on some bit of cluster/VPC configuration)
- IPv4:
  - for each NIC:
    - append all IPv4 IPs on the NIC as InternalIPs
    - for each of ExternalIP, InternalDNS, HostName, and ExternalDNS:
      - if the NIC has one of those associated with it, append it
- IPv6:
  - for each NIC:
    - append only the first IPv6 IP on the NIC as an InternalIP

Depending on the cluster configuration, GetNodeHostIPs may return just an IPv4 IP, just an IPv6 IP, an IPv4 IP followed by an IPv6 IP, or an IPv6 IP followed by an IPv4 IP. In all cases, the IPv4 IP will be the first IPv4 IP on the first NIC that has any IPv4 IPs and the IPv6 IP will be the first IPv6 IP on the first NIC that has any IPv6 IPs.

LoadBalancers are pointed at VMs. The [AWS docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-target-groups.html) say:

> If you specify targets using an instance ID, traffic is routed to instances using the primary private IP address that is specified in the primary network interface for the instance.

and

> When registering targets by instance ID for a IPv6 target group, the targets must have an assigned primary IPv6 address.

The most plausible reading of this is that it corresponds to our primary node IPs.

### Azure

[`node.Status.Addresses` is constructed as](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cloud-provider-azure/blob/v1.29.3/pkg/provider/azure_instances_v1.go#L110-L153)
- append HostName
- if the first NIC has a private IPv4 IP, then
  - append the private IPv4 IP as an InternalIP
  - if it also has a public IPv4 IP then append it as an ExternalIP
- if the first NIC has a private IPv6 IP, then
  - append the private IPv6 IP as an InternalIP
  - if it also has a public IPv6 IP then append it as an ExternalIP

So this supports single-stack IPv4, single-stack IPv6, and dual-stack IPv4-primary, but not dual-stack IPv6-primary. In all cases, if GetNodeHostIPs returns an IPv4 IP it will be the private IPv4 IP of the first NIC, and if it returns an IPv6 IP, it will be the private IPv6 IP of the first NIC.

Unlike GCE and AWS, [the loadbalancer code configures loadbalancers using IPs](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cloud-provider-azure/blob/v1.29.3/pkg/provider/azure_loadbalancer_backendpool.go#L446-L471), where the function [`getNodePrivateIPAddress`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cloud-provider-azure/blob/v1.29.3/pkg/provider/azure_utils.go#L201) pulls IPs out of the `node.Status.Addresses`, taking the first InternalIP of the desired IP family. So it will always route to the IPs we consider the primary node IPs.

### vSphere

[`node.Status.Addresses` is constructed as](https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-vsphere/blob/master/pkg/cloudprovider/vsphere/nodemanager.go#L276-L356):
- append HostName
- (create a list of all IPs on the node, sorted by NIC ifindex and by the order of addresses on each NIC, and then eliminate various "unusable" IPs, including IPs in ranges that the configuration says should never be used as the node IP.)
- for each IP family (in an order determined by cluster/network config):
  - if there is a usable IP on some NIC that appears to match the configuration's idea of an "internal network" IP, then append the first such IP as an InternalIP
  - if there is a usable IP on some NIC that appears to match the configuration's idea of an "external network" IP, then append the first such IP as an ExternalIP
  - if no IPs match according to configuration, then append the first usable IP on any NIC as both InternalIP and ExternalIP

(Note that this doesn't match [what I said about vSphere above](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123105#discussion_r1513190698); they've improved things since the last time I looked at it.)

Anyway, "it's complicated", and it can result in any single or dual stack GetNodeHostIPs result.

Load balancers are handled basically the same as Azure; the CloudProvider tells vSphere which IPs to use, not which VMs, and it [pulls those IPs out of `node.Status.Addresses`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cloud-provider-azure/blob/v1.29.3/pkg/provider/azure_utils.go#L201), using the first InternalIP value for each node. Unlike the Azure code, it doesn't take IP family into account, suggesting limited support for dual-stack LoadBalancers. But anyway, loadbalancer traffic gets sent to what we consider the primary node IP.

### Notes

None of the CloudProviders above ever add an ExternalIP of a given IP family without having previously added an InternalIP of the same family, meaning the "or else ExternalIP" fallback case in GetNodeHostIPs never gets hit (for these CloudProviders).

In all the cases except Azure, the cloud provider code seems to support the possibility of a node with primary IPv4 and IPv6 IPs on different NICs, assuming the underlying cloud lets you do that. (This could certainly happen in vSphere.)

Anyway, I didn't investigate any other providers, but it seems like the "loadbalancers target the primary node IPs" assumption is reasonable.

> Anyway, I didn't investigate any other providers, but it seems like the "loadbalancers target the primary node IPs" assumption is reasonable.

GCE. is way more complicated like that as there are many flavors of loadbalancers, the L4 LBs add a "virtual IP" to the nodes and send traffic there, there are others LBs that target the PodIPs directly ...  however, this behavior is implemented for one of the modes

https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-gce/blob/a34a81099bf4258b4544a2527b9f3c232d77d6ca/pkg/utils/utils.go#L581-L582

>  "loadbalancers target the primary node IPs" assumption is reasonable.

agree, and since this is and opt-in feature , for more complex scenarios people can just fall back to previous behavior, no?

> > it seems like the "loadbalancers target the primary node IPs" assumption is reasonable.
> 
> GCE is way more complicated like that as there are many flavors of loadbalancers

Meh, I was only looking at CloudProvider-provided LoadBalancers, not official ingress mechanisms.

> the L4 LBs add a "virtual IP" to the nodes and send traffic there, there are others LBs that target the PodIPs directly

If they're not sending traffic to NodePorts or HealthCheckNodePorts than nothing they do will be affected by this new option. Hopefully any LB that *does* send to nodeports is using the primary node IPs?

> and since this is and opt-in feature , for more complex scenarios people can just fall back to previous behavior, no?

well, it's (already) the default for nftables, though as noted in the release note, you can say `--nodeport-addresses 0.0.0.0/0,::/0` to get the old kube-proxy behavior under nftables.

(oops, didn't notice the codegen comment until too late; needs another push)
I ended up reorganizing `checkBadConfig` vs `checkBadIPConfig` a little more (to put the NodePortAddresses checking entirely into the former, rather than being split between the two). Yes, this is kind of a mess but it will all have to be revisited when we add the `--config-hard-fail` option (to make all bad configuration fatal) with v1alpha2 anyway

issue_context.title: Service NodePorts can be accessed via LB IPs (iptables, at least)
issue_context.body:
Create a single-port Service of type LB.  It gets nodeport 31234.

Wait for an LB IP to be assigned.

Access that LB IP on 31234 - it works as long as firewalls don't stop it.

This is because the NodPorts chain doesn't necessarily check IPs (hence why it is the last chain).  It finds port 31234 and forwards it to the Service.

I think we need to add rules to "KUBE-PROXY-FIREWALL" to allow valid IP+port combos and then drop other uses of those IPs.  Or something.

@danwinship since you are elbow-deep in that area.

This problem does not exist for proxy-mode=ipvs.
```
vm-201 ~ # curl http://192.168.1.2:30018 > /dev/null
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
100   232  100   232    0     0  36907      0 --:--:-- --:--:-- --:--:-- 38666
vm-201 ~ # curl http://10.0.0.80:30018  > /dev/null
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
  0     0    0     0    0     0      0      0 --:--:-- --:--:-- --:--:--     0
curl: (7) Failed to connect to 10.0.0.80 port 30018 after 2 ms: Connection refused
```
192.168.1.2 is a node address and 10.0.0.80 is a LB-address.

So, we _can_ work around this in kube-proxy, but I believe this bug is a side effect of GCE stuff which is not part of core Kubernetes. The rule that iptables kube-proxy creates to jump to the nodeports chain is:

    -A KUBE-SERVICES -m comment --comment "kubernetes service nodeports; NOTE: this must be the last rule in this chain"
        -m addrtype --dst-type LOCAL -j KUBE-NODEPORTS

`--dst-type LOCAL` means it will only match for packets that are addressed to an IP which the routing table considers to be local (meaning either the IP is assigned to a local interface, or there is an `ip route` rule intercepting traffic for that IP and delivering it to a local interface). Neither iptables kube-proxy nor the GCP CloudProvider adds LB IPs as local IPs, or adds routes directing LB IP traffic to the local host, so this rule _should not match_ LB IP traffic unless something besides core Kubernetes is mucking with the routing of LB IP traffic.

I know in OpenShift-on-GCP, there _is_ a service that does special handling for LoadBalancer IPs, and I'm pretty sure it's a fork of something that runs on GCE. The behavior in OpenShift has changed over the years, and it now uses iptables rules rather than routes, but it ends up having [the same bug](https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=2094408) (which I had assumed GCE _didn't_ have), and my conclusion there was that we shouldn't be running that script for LB IPs that correspond to Kubernetes Services; it should only be used for LB IPs that _aren't_ being managed by kube-proxy. (Of course if there are LB IPs that are used for both kube-proxy-managed Services and for other things, then that rule wouldn't work...)

Assuming I'm right and this service does exist in GCE, we should probably document its existence and behavior better in the kube-proxy code/docs...
note: all implementations that add IP addresses to the node may be affected by this, per example, platforms that use Keepalived on nodes for ExternalIPs  or LoadBalancer IPs

Yeah, any LB implementation that is VIP-ish should have this problem - something needs to accept VIP traffic locally.

My fear is that we end up with 1 "ALLOW" `filter` rule for every service-ip-port and then final "DROP" rules, increasing the number of iptables rules.  With things like `externalIPs` it's not even obvious when to put that rule, since a single externalIP could be used on multiple Services (with disjoint sets of ports).  Also, annoyingly, this speaks to the value of KUBE-MARK-DROP, since we already enumerate all service-ip-ports in `nat`.

> My fear is that we end up with 1 "ALLOW" filter rule for every service-ip-port and then final "DROP" rules, increasing the number of iptables rules

Tim mentioned briefly in the meeting that we have all these problems with bad Service defaults, and I feel like part of the answer here might be to encourage people to use `--nodeport-addresses` or something similar; then we can just change the `KUBE-NODEPORTS` jump rule to only match traffic on those IPs, rather than having to un-match everything else.

(Also, if people use a `--nodeport-addresses` that doesn't include 127.0.0.1 then we can also get rid of the localhost-nodeport junk.)

But even without that, we still don't need 1 rule per IP; we can just make the iptables proxy use ipsets like the ipvs proxy does... there's no real reason other than "history" for why it doesn't.

> encourage people to use `--nodeport-addresses` or something similar

eg
`klog.Warning("--nodeport-addresses not specified; NodePorts will be available on all local IPs!")`
yeah, the `Access that LB IP on 31234 - it works as long as firewalls don't stop it.`  is totally valid if the LB IP belong to the Node ... but is this new? this should be always working like this
Yes, it always worked like this, but it was never _intended_ to work like this.

If we added `--nodeport-addresses node-ip` meaning "only accept NodePort connections on the node's primary IP (of the relevant IP family)", would that work with the various cloud load balancers that actually use NodePorts? If not, would it work if we had it mean "only accept NodePort connections on IPs in `node.Status.Addresses`"? (Yes, in both cases it would imply "no NodePorts on localhost"; people who want localhost NodePorts would have to continue not using `--nodeport-addresses` or else specify the right IP/CIDR by hand.)

#123105 implements the suggestion above, of adding a new option to request that NodePorts only work on the node's primary IP, and it adds a warning if you don't use that option and don't manually set `--nodeport-addresses`.

Additionally, the nftables backend implements that functionality by default (#122724) and we should update the `v1alpha2.KubeProxyConfiguration` plan (https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/4337) to enable this by default as well.
